\noindent\textbf{Running title:} \psmcrs: fast, reproducible PSMC\\
\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} demographic inference, effective population size, PSMC, coalescent hidden Markov model, reproducibility, software

\linenumbers
\onehalfspacing

\begin{abstract}
\noindent The pairwise sequentially Markovian coalescent (PSMC) infers the history of effective population size from one diploid genome and is one of the most widely used methods of population genomics, but its reference implementation runs on one thread. We present \psmcrs{}, a reimplementation of PSMC in Rust that fits the same model as the C program. Fitted to the same inputs (\EoneGenomes{} simulated and \RealGenomes{} real genomes), \psmcrs{} and C psmc gave population size histories that differed by a root-mean-square of at most \EtwoRsCRmseMax{} in $\log_{10}\Ne$; on the simulated genomes this difference was at least \EoneFoldMin{} times smaller than either program's error. On a \EthreeBigMb{}~Mb genome, \psmcrs{} was \EthreeSpeedOne{} times as fast as C psmc on one thread and up to \EthreeSpeedThirty{} times as fast on 30 threads, used \EthreeRsMemOne{}~MB of memory instead of \EthreeCMem{}~MB, and gave byte-identical results on any number of threads. Fitting all \EsevenGenomes{} unrelated high-coverage genomes of the 1000 Genomes Project took \psmcrs{} \EsevenRsCoreHours{} core-hours, where C psmc would have needed about \EsevenCCoreHoursAll{}. \psmcrs{} also reads VCF and multihetsep files, accounts for partly callable sequence, and runs C psmc's bootstrap in parallel. It is open source under the MIT license; the pipeline that produced every result, and the inputs and fits of the \EsevenGenomes{} genomes, are openly available.
\end{abstract}

\section*{Introduction}

The pairwise sequentially Markovian coalescent \citep[PSMC;][]{li2011} infers how the effective size (\Ne) of a population changed over time from the two genome copies of one diploid individual. It treats the time to the most recent common ancestor (TMRCA) of the two copies, which changes along the genome at recombination events, as the hidden state of a hidden Markov model whose observations are short bins of sequence, heterozygous or homozygous, and fits a piecewise-constant history of \Ne{} by expectation--maximization. Because it needs only one unphased genome, PSMC has been applied to modern and archaic humans \citep{li2011,prufer2014,mallick2016} and to a wide range of other species \citep{nadachowska2016,hilgers2025}, and it remains the reference for newer coalescent hidden Markov models \citep{schiffels2014,terhorst2017,cousins2025,terhorst2025}.

The reference implementation, the C program \texttt{psmc} \citep{psmcC}, runs on one thread: 25 iterations on a 3~Gb genome take more than an hour, a bootstrap multiplies that by its replicates, and population resources such as the high-coverage 1000 Genomes data \citep{byrskabishop2022} now hold thousands of genomes. Other programs port PSMC to other languages and toolkits \citep{psmcr,psmcpython,smckit} or extend its model \citep{schiffels2020,liu2022,cousins2024,cousins2025}. To replace C psmc, however, a faster program must also reproduce its results, so that new analyses remain comparable with the many PSMC curves already published.

Here we present \psmcrs{}, a reimplementation of PSMC in Rust. We show that it reproduces C psmc's fits of simulated and real genomes, that it is an order of magnitude faster on one thread and two orders faster on many, with a fraction of the memory and with results that do not depend on the number of threads, and we apply it to all \EsevenGenomes{} unrelated high-coverage genomes of the 1000 Genomes Project, whose inputs and fits we release.

\section*{Results}

\subsection*{\psmcrs{}}

\psmcrs{} fits the PSMC model of \citet{li2011} as C psmc 0.6.5 implements it: the same discretization of time, the same transition and emission probabilities, the same parameter patterns and starting point, and expectation--maximization of the same objective (Methods). It reads C psmc's \texttt{psmcfa} files, VCF files (all-sites consensus calls, or variant calls with a mask of callable sites) and MSMC's multihetsep files, and it writes the fitted model as JSON, an HTML report and, on request, C psmc's \texttt{.psmc} output, which \texttt{psmc\_plot.pl} draws. With the settings of C psmc's documentation, a human genome is fitted on eight threads by
\begin{verbatim}
psmc-rs NA12878.psmcfa.gz NA12878.json 25 --pattern 4+25*2+4+6 --t-max 15 \
    --tr-ratio 5 --mu 1.25e-8 --gen-years 29 --threads 8 --psmc-out NA12878.psmc
\end{verbatim}
\psmcrs{} differs from C psmc in four ways (Methods): it processes the sequences of a genome in parallel, each on one thread; its M-step maximizes with L-BFGS to convergence, within bounds on the parameters, instead of with a Hooke--Jeeves search; it counts the last bin of each sequence, which C psmc leaves out; and, when the input records it, it weights each bin by the number of its bases that are callable.

\subsection*{\psmcrs{} reproduces C psmc}

We fitted both programs, with the same inputs and settings, to \EoneGenomes{} simulated genomes of \EoneGenomeMb{}~Mb, ten under each of \EoneModelsW{} demographic models, and to \RealGenomes{} real genomes: \EtwoTurtlesW{} turtles and \EsevenDefault{} human genomes of the 1000 Genomes Project (Methods). On every genome the two programs' histories agreed to an RMSE of at most \EtwoRsCRmseMax{} in $\log_{10}\Ne$ over the informative window, the times between the 1\% and 99\% quantiles of the pairwise coalescence time (Table~\ref{tab:agreement}, Fig.~\ref{fig:agree}). Over the \AgreeIntervals{} intervals of these \AgreeGenomes{} fits, the two programs' \Ne{} differed by a median of \AgreeMedianAbs{} and at most \AgreeMaxAbs{} in $\log_{10}\Ne$, or \AgreeMaxPct{} (Fig.~\ref{fig:agree}i). On the simulated genomes the difference, \EoneRsCRmseMin{} to \EoneRsCRmseMax{}, was at least \EoneFoldMin{} times smaller than either program's error relative to the true history, and \EoneFoldMedian{} times smaller between the medians (Fig.~\ref{fig:agree}j); the programs shared that error to three decimals: on average \EoneConstantTruthRs{} for the constant-size model and up to \EoneBottleneckTruthRs{} for the bottleneck (Table~S1).

At the shared starting point the first E-step gave log-likelihoods equal to a relative \EoneLoglikeFirstRelMax{}, so the two programs evaluate the same likelihood; their small differences arise during the iterations. A diagnostic on a test genome (Methods) traced them not to the M-step's optimizer but to the last bin of each sequence: leaving that bin out of \psmcrs{}'s expected counts, as C psmc does, brought the curves from \DiagCurve{} to within \DiagLastBin{} of C psmc's, whereas C psmc's Hooke--Jeeves search in place of L-BFGS left them \DiagHookeJeeves{} apart. In line with this, of the turtles and NA12878, the RMSE was smallest for NA12878, with \EtwoHumanSequences{} sequences, and largest for the turtle \textit{Pelusios castaneus}, with \EtwoTurtleSeqMax{} (Fig.~\ref{fig:agree}e--h). The bootstrap of each of these genomes by \psmcrs{} refitted its main fit exactly, and its 95\% bands held both programs' curves (Fig.~\ref{fig:agree}e--h). In both programs the log-likelihood never decreased from one iteration to the next (Fig.~S1). Outside the informative window, where the data say little, the programs can disagree: in one of the \EoneGenomes{} simulated genomes, the first free $\lambda$, the relative size of the four most recent intervals, ran away in both, to \psmcrs{}'s upper bound of $10^4$ and, unbounded, to \EoneRunawayC{} in C psmc. The turtles' curves also show recent peaks (Fig.~\ref{fig:agree}f--h), artefacts of this pattern's first time window that \citet{hilgers2025} found in many published curves: splitting the window into two or four free $\lambda$s removed them in all \EtwoSplitFitsW{} fits and raised the log-likelihood by \EtwoSplitGainMin{} to \EtwoSplitGainMax{} units.

\subsection*{\psmcrs{} is fast, lean and deterministic}

We timed both programs on constant-size genomes of 1, 3, 10 and 30 chromosomes of 100~Mb, each run alone on an exclusive node, with \EthreeRepeatsW{} repeats on \EthreeNodesW{} nodes (Fig.~\ref{fig:perf}, Table~\ref{tab:timing}). On \EthreeBigMb{}~Mb, 25 iterations took C psmc \EthreeCWall{}~s (\EthreeCMin{} minutes) and \psmcrs{} \EthreeRsOneWall{}~s on one thread, \EthreeSpeedOne{} times as fast (\EthreeSpeedOneMin{} to \EthreeSpeedOneMax{} at every size; Fig.~\ref{fig:perf}a). With its sequences in parallel, \psmcrs{} was \EthreeSpeedEight{}, \EthreeSpeedSixteen{} and \EthreeSpeedThirty{} times as fast as C psmc on 8, 16 and 30 threads, with a parallel efficiency of \EthreeEffMin{} to \EthreeEffMax{} on 2 to 30 threads (Fig.~\ref{fig:perf}b), and fitted the \EthreeBigMb{}~Mb genome in \EthreeRsWallThirty{}~s. Because each sequence runs on one thread, the longest sequence bounds the speed-up: one 100~Mb chromosome took \EthreeChromWallMin{} to \EthreeChromWallMax{}~s on 1, 8 and 30 threads alike, and the 30-thread speed-up holds because the genome has 30 chromosomes. \psmcrs{} needed \EthreeRsMemOne{}~MB of memory on one thread and \EthreeRsMemThirty{}~MB on 30, against \EthreeCMem{}~MB for C psmc (Fig.~\ref{fig:perf}c), because it keeps the forward pass of the E-step only at checkpoints and recomputes the rest (Methods).

\psmcrs{}'s results do not depend on the number of threads. At each genome size, its fitted models from every thread count, repeat and node, \EthreeDetRsTotal{} in all, were byte-identical, as were C psmc's \EthreeDetCTotal{} outputs. The bootstrap of NA12878, run with one seed on \EtwoBootThreads{} and on \EsevenBootThreads{} threads, wrote \EsevenBootFilesIdentical{} of \EsevenBootFiles{} files byte for byte the same. Between platforms, results differ only in their last digits: refitted on a laptop of another processor architecture, operating system and mathematical library, the \EoneGenomes{} simulated genomes gave curves within an RMSE of \XpRsRmseMax{} in $\log_{10}\Ne$ of the cluster's, a median of \XpRatioCMedian{} times closer than two builds of C psmc on the same two machines (Supplementary Note~1, section~9).

\subsection*{Partly callable sequence, bootstrap and decoding}

Beyond reproducing C psmc, \psmcrs{} accounts for bins of sequence that are only partly callable. \texttt{fq2psmcfa}, which makes C psmc's input, marks a 100~bp bin missing only when more than 90\% of its bases are uncallable, so a bin with a few uncallable bases is fitted as if all of them had been observed, which biases PSMC's estimates \citep{lipson2015,nadachowska2016}. When the input records how many of a bin's bases are callable, as a VCF with its callable mask does, \psmcrs{} weights the bin by them (Methods), as recent coalescent hidden Markov models do \citep{cousins2024,cousins2025}. In simulated genomes with 30\% of positions uncallable in short runs, the standard route underestimated the scaled mutation rate by \EfourDispThirtyFqTheta{}, and every size and time with it, whereas the weighted fit was \EfourDispThirtyAutoTheta{} low (Fig.~S2). Inputs that record no callable bases, such as \texttt{psmcfa} files, are fitted with C psmc's model unchanged.

\psmcrs{} runs C psmc's block bootstrap in parallel, each replicate with its own random stream, so that a seed gives the same replicates on any number of threads. In a calibration study of a bottleneck model, the bootstrap's 95\% bands covered the mean of independent fits at \EfiveFiftyCovMean{} to \EfiveFiveCovMean{} of times but the true history at only \EfiveFiftyCov{} to \EfiveFiveCov{}: they measure the sampling variation of an estimate, not PSMC's bias (Fig.~S3). \psmcrs{} also fits a genome read as \texttt{psmcfa} and as VCF identically, decodes the posterior distribution of the TMRCA of every bin, whose central 95\% held the true TMRCA in \EsixDecodeCov{} of simulated bins, and checks every input before fitting it (\opt{psmc-rs qc}).

\subsection*{2,504 human genomes}

We applied \psmcrs{} to all \EsevenGenomes{} unrelated individuals of the high-coverage 1000 Genomes data \citep{byrskabishop2022}: \EsevenPops{} populations of \EsevenPerPopMin{} to \EsevenPerPopMax{} individuals, sequenced to a median depth of \EsevenDepth{}$\times$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:kg}). From the joint-called VCFs we made one \texttt{psmcfa} file per genome with the strict accessibility mask, and with the position of every record that failed the callset's filters set missing (Methods); against Genome in a Bottle's benchmark for NA12878 \citep{zook2019,wagner2022}, the heterozygous single-nucleotide sites of its input had a precision of \EsevenGiabPrecision{} and a recall of \EsevenGiabRecall{}. With one fit per thread on a shared node, \psmcrs{} took a median of \EsevenRsFitMin{} minutes per genome and \EsevenRsCoreHours{} core-hours for the cohort. C psmc, run the same way on a default set of \EsevenDefault{} genomes (two per population), took a median of \EsevenCFitMin{} minutes per genome, which would make about \EsevenCCoreHoursAll{} core-hours for the cohort. On those \EsevenDefault{} genomes the two programs agreed to an RMSE of \EsevenRsCRmseMin{} to \EsevenRsCRmseMax{} in $\log_{10}\Ne$ (Table~\ref{tab:agreement}).

The histories have the features of published single-genome PSMC analyses of human genomes \citep{li2011,prufer2014,mallick2016} (Fig.~\ref{fig:kg}a). The median curves of the four superpopulations outside Africa fell to \EsevenNonAfrMinNeLo{} to \EsevenNonAfrMinNeHi{} between \EsevenNonAfrMinKyLo{} and \EsevenNonAfrMinKyHi{} thousand years ago, while the African median declined only to \EsevenAfrMinNe{}, and from \EsevenConvergeKy{} thousand years ago to the end of the window, \EsevenWindowHiMy{} million years ago, the five superpopulations' curves were within 20\% of one another. Within each superpopulation, the populations' curves differed by up to \EsevenPopSpreadRecentLo{} to \EsevenPopSpreadRecentHi{} in $\log_{10}\Ne$ in the last \EsevenPopCutKy{} thousand years, in the depth of the bottleneck and in the rise after it, and by at most \EsevenPopSpreadOldMax{} before (Fig.~\ref{fig:kg}b--f). Fitted from their VCFs with each bin weighted by its callable bases, the \EsevenDefault{} default genomes gave a scaled mutation rate \EsevenThetaShift{} higher, close to the \EsevenThetaExpected{} expected from the \EsevenMissingShare{} of called bins' bases that are uncallable, with the populations' order and shapes unchanged. The \texttt{psmcfa} inputs and the fits of all \EsevenGenomes{} genomes are released as a resource (Data availability).

\section*{Discussion}

\psmcrs{} reproduces C psmc's PSMC fits. On the same inputs its histories differ from C psmc's by far less than the method's own error, and the remaining difference traces to a bookkeeping choice, the last bin of each sequence. Analyses of the same input files can therefore move to \psmcrs{}, and repeat or extend published PSMC analyses, without their conclusions changing because of the program. \psmcrs{} is an order of magnitude faster than C psmc on one thread and two orders faster on many, needs tens of megabytes of memory rather than a gigabyte, and its results do not depend on the number of threads, which makes cohorts of thousands of genomes, and bootstraps of every genome, practical.

\psmcrs{} keeps PSMC's model, and with it PSMC's limits. One genome says little about the last few thousand generations, where the first free $\lambda$ can run away (\psmcrs{} bounds it and warns when it does); ancestral population structure can produce changes in a single-genome curve that are not changes in size \citep{mazet2016,cousins2025}; and methods that combine many genomes, such as MSMC2 \citep{schiffels2020}, SMC++ \citep{terhorst2017} or PHLASH \citep{terhorst2025}, resolve recent times better. The bootstrap describes sampling variation, not these biases (Fig.~S3). Because \psmcrs{} parallelizes across sequences, a genome assembled into a few long sequences gains less from many threads than one of many sequences. \psmcrs{} does not replace methods for many genomes; it makes the single-genome reference fast and reproducible.

\section*{Methods}

\subsection*{Model}

\psmcrs{} fits the model of \citet{li2011} with the conventions of C psmc 0.6.5-r74 \citep{psmcC}. Time is measured in units of $2N_0$ generations and divided into $n+1$ intervals $[t_k,t_{k+1})$, with $t_k=\alpha(e^{\beta k}-1)$ for $k=0,\dots,n-1$, $\beta=\ln(1+t_{\max}/\alpha)/n$, $\alpha=0.1$, $t_n=t_{\max}$ and $t_{n+1}$ a large value standing for infinity (1,000, as in C psmc). The population size in interval $k$ is $\lambda_kN_0$. The free parameters are the scaled mutation rate $\theta$ and recombination rate $\rho$ per bin, $t_{\max}$, and the free $\lambda$s, each spanning consecutive intervals according to a pattern: \opt{4+25*2+4+6} has 64 intervals and 28 free $\lambda$s, the first spanning the four most recent intervals. The initial distribution, the transition probabilities and the expected coalescence time $\bar t_k$ in each interval are computed exactly as C psmc computes them (\psmcrs{}'s code is a line-by-line port of its \texttt{psmc\_update\_hmm}). A bin is heterozygous (K) if it holds a heterozygous site, homozygous (T) otherwise, or missing (N), with emission probabilities $e_T(k)=e^{-\theta\bar t_k}$, $e_K(k)=1-e_T(k)$ and $e_N(k)=1$. Sizes and times are scaled with a mutation rate $\mu$ per bp per generation, the bin size $s$ and a generation time $g$: $N_0=\theta/(4\mu s)$, $\Ne=\lambda_kN_0$, and a time $t$ is $2N_0tg$ years.

When the input records how many of a bin's $s$ bases are callable, $c$, \psmcrs{} uses
\begin{equation}
P(T\mid k,c)=e_T(k)^{c/s}=e^{-\theta\bar t_k c/s},\qquad P(K\mid k,c)=1-P(T\mid k,c),
\end{equation}
the probability that $c$ callable bases hold no heterozygous site under the Poisson bin likelihood of cobraa and PSMC+ \citep{cousins2025,cousins2024}, restricted to PSMC's binary observations (\opt{--bin-callable auto}, the default). Full bins, and inputs without counts, are fitted with C psmc's model. A VCF read with a callable mask gives $c$ as $s$ minus the bin's positions outside the mask, inside a negative mask, at records that failed the callset's filters, with a missing or partial genotype, or in the reference span of a heterozygous variant that is not a single-nucleotide variant. Bins follow \texttt{fq2psmcfa}'s rule: missing if more than 90\% of their bases are, heterozygous if any callable site is heterozygous, homozygous otherwise.

\subsection*{Inference}

\paragraph{E-step.} The forward--backward algorithm runs in double precision on each sequence, with the forward vector normalized at every bin; the log-likelihood is the sum of the logarithms of the normalizers. To bound memory, the forward pass is kept every 128 bins and the bins between these checkpoints are recomputed, to the same bits, during the backward pass. For models of up to 256 states the forward and backward passes take time linear in the number of states, from the rank-one structure of PSMC's transition matrix \citep{harris2014}; the expected transition counts take quadratic time. The expected counts include the last bin of every sequence, which C psmc leaves out. On x86-64 processors with AVX2 and FMA, \psmcrs{} chooses kernels compiled for them when it starts, and portable kernels otherwise; on aarch64 it uses NEON kernels. The JSON output and the HTML report record which kernels ran.

\paragraph{M-step.} \psmcrs{} maximizes C psmc's objective, the expected complete-data log-likelihood of the transitions and emissions, over all free parameters with L-BFGS \citep{liu1989}, with a memory of 20, an Armijo line search and gradients from a hand-written adjoint, on logits within the bounds $\theta,\rho\in[10^{-12},10]$ per bin, $t_{\max}\in[1,200]$ and $\lambda\in[10^{-6},10^4]$. It stops when two consecutive iterations decrease the objective, and predict a decrease, by at most $10^{-13}$ of its value, when its line search fails after up to three restarts, or after 1,000 iterations. C psmc instead uses a Hooke--Jeeves direct search \citep{hooke1961} on unbounded parameters. EM starts, as C psmc's does, from $\theta_0=-\ln(1-K/L)$, with $K$ the heterozygous and $L$ the non-missing bins (with callable counts, the root of $\sum_i(1-e^{-\theta_0c_i/s})=K$), $\rho_0=\theta_0/r$ (\opt{--tr-ratio}, 4 by default), $t_{\max}$ (\opt{--t-max}, 15) and every $\lambda=1$. The residual difference from C psmc was traced on a simulated genome of \DiagChroms{}$\times$\DiagChromMb{}~Mb with builds modified for this diagnostic, which are not part of the release (repository README, section ``Testing and C equivalence''): \psmcrs{}'s default fit was within \DiagPrecision{} of one whose M-steps ran to the limit of precision, and each of the two changes described in Results was made alone.

\paragraph{Parallelism and determinism.} The E-step and the log-likelihood run in parallel over work items, contiguous groups of whole sequences whose grouping depends only on the number of sequences; partial sums are merged in the order of the items, so they do not depend on which thread finished first. The M-step is serial. The bootstrap follows C psmc: it cuts each sequence into blocks of 500,000 bins as \texttt{splitfa} does, a remainder shorter than 1.5 blocks staying in the last block, and each replicate draws blocks with replacement as C psmc's \texttt{psmc\_resamp} does, starting afresh from its own $\theta_0$. Replicates run in parallel, each drawing from its own ChaCha8 stream seeded from the bootstrap seed and its index. Posterior decoding (\opt{--tmrca-out}) gives, for every bin, the posterior mean TMRCA, the most probable state and the states at which the posterior reaches 2.5\% and 97.5\%.

\subsection*{Experiments}

All results come from one pipeline (\texttt{experiment/pipeline}) that simulates the genomes, runs both programs with matched settings, records how every output was made and draws every figure from its tables; Supplementary Note~1 describes how to reproduce them. Both programs fitted 25 EM iterations with the command of C psmc's documentation, \texttt{psmc -N25 -t15 -r5 -p "4+25*2+4+6"}, whose pattern and maximum time are those \citet{li2011} used for human genomes, and \psmcrs{} 0.2.0 with the matching options, on 100~bp bins and one thread unless stated otherwise. Every seed was fixed in advance, from the SHA-256 of a string naming the experiment, model, replicate and stage.

\paragraph{Comparisons.} The fits of the two programs to the same input have the same intervals, whose boundaries differ in years only through $\theta$ and $t_{\max}$, and are compared interval by interval: for each interval $k$ of C psmc's fit that overlaps the window $[a,b]$, $d_k=\log_{10}(N^{\text{rs}}_k/N^{\text{C}}_k)$, where $N^{\text{rs}}_k$ and $N^{\text{C}}_k$ are the two fits' \Ne{} in interval $k$, weighted by $w_k=\ln(\min(e_k,b)/\max(s_k,a))$ for an interval from $s_k$ to $e_k$; the RMSE is $(\sum_kw_kd_k^2/\sum_kw_k)^{1/2}$. The window spans the 1\% to 99\% quantiles of the pairwise coalescence time under the true model (simulations) or under the fitted one (C psmc's where the programs are compared, \psmcrs{}'s otherwise). Fits of different inputs, whose $\theta$ and time scales differ by percents, are compared at the same times. A fit is compared with the truth by the RMSE of $\log_{10}\Ne$ over 200 log-spaced times in the window.

\paragraph{Simulated genomes (E1; Fig.~\ref{fig:agree}, Table~S1, Fig.~S1).} Four models, in diploid sizes and generations: constant size 10,000; a bottleneck (20,000 for 0--800 generations, 1,000 to 1,200, 10,000 to 4,000, 5,000 to 40,000, then 10,000); an expansion (10,000 for 0--400 generations, 1,000 to 2,400, 10,000 to 8,000, 5,000 to 40,000, 10,000 to 80,000, then 20,000); and the zigzag model of \citet{schiffels2014} from stdpopsim 0.3.0 \citep{adrion2020}. Each of \EoneReps{} replicates per model was \EoneChroms{} unlinked chromosomes of \EoneChromMb{}~Mb, simulated for one diploid individual with msprime 1.4.4 \citep{kelleher2016,baumdicker2022} under the coalescent with recombination, with $\mu=2.5\times10^{-8}$ and $r=10^{-8}$ per bp per generation, and scaled with $g=25$ years.

\paragraph{Real genomes (E2; Fig.~\ref{fig:agree}e--h).} NA12878's \texttt{psmcfa} file is the one made for E7 (below). The turtle \texttt{psmcfa} files are \placeholder{source of the turtle data}. The turtles were scaled with $\mu=4.6\times10^{-9}$, the mean of nine trios of the painted turtle \citep{bergeron2023}, and $g=15$ years, close to the generation times that \citet{sozzoni2025} used for two of the species; NA12878 with $\mu=1.25\times10^{-8}$ \citep{scally2012} and $g=29$ years \citep{fenner2005}. Each genome was bootstrapped with \EtwoBootReps{} replicates of 50~Mb blocks on \EtwoBootThreads{} threads, and the turtles were refitted with the pattern's first window split into two (\opt{2+2+25*2+4+6}) or four (\opt{1+1+1+1+25*2+4+6}) free $\lambda$s.

\paragraph{Performance (E3; Fig.~\ref{fig:perf}, Table~\ref{tab:timing}).} Genomes of 1, 3, 10 and 30 chromosomes of 100~Mb were simulated under constant size. C psmc ran on one thread and \psmcrs{} on 1, 8 and 30 threads, and also on 2, 4 and 16 threads on 3,000~Mb: \EthreeSetups{} setups of \EthreeRepeatsW{} repeats, each repeat on its own exclusive \EthreeCpu{} node. Before each run the node had to be quiet, with at most one core and 10\% of cores busy over 2~s; during the run, other processes could use at most 0.5 core and 5\% of cores, or the run was repeated later. Peak memory is the larger of the program's \texttt{ru\_maxrss} and its process tree's resident memory sampled every 0.5~s. Outputs (C psmc's \texttt{.psmc}, \psmcrs{}'s JSON) were compared byte for byte with the same program's output on the fewest threads in the first repeat.

\paragraph{Partly callable sequence, bootstrap and decoding (E4--E6; Figs S2 and S3).} E4 masked \EfourRepsW{} bottleneck genomes of E1's size with uncallable runs of mean \EfourClusRunKb{}~kb (clustered) or \EfourDispRunBp{}~bp (dispersed) covering 10\% or 30\% of positions, and compared \psmcrs{} on the VCF with its mask, with and without weighting, a consensus sequence converted by \texttt{fq2psmcfa} (which gave the unweighted fit exactly), multihetsep, and the VCF without its mask, against the fit of the same genome without missing data. E5 simulated \EfiveFits{} bottleneck genomes of \EfiveChroms{}$\times$50~Mb, fitted each, and bootstrapped \EfiveDatasets{} of them with \EfiveReps{} replicates, with blocks of 50 and 5~Mb; coverage has Clopper--Pearson intervals \citep{clopper1934}. E6 read E1's first replicate of each model as \texttt{psmcfa}, VCF and multihetsep; decoded E1's first bottleneck replicate with its fitted model (\opt{--tmrca-out} on 4 threads) against its true TMRCA, re-simulated from the recorded seeds; and ran \opt{psmc-rs qc} on E2's genomes.

\paragraph{1000 Genomes (E7; Fig.~\ref{fig:kg}).} The inputs were the joint-called VCFs of the 3,202 high-coverage samples \citep{byrskabishop2022} for chromosomes 1--22 (\EsevenRecords{} records), of which we used the \EsevenGenomes{} unrelated individuals; the GRCh38 strict accessibility mask; and, as a negative mask shared by all samples, the position of every record whose FILTER was neither PASS nor `.' (\EsevenNonpass{} records). Each chromosome was downloaded and checked against its published size and MD5 checksum, read in chunks of 15~Mb with \texttt{bcftools} 1.24 \citep{danecek2021} and split into one VCF per sample of its heterozygous or missing genotypes; \opt{psmc-rs convert --vcf-mode mask} then wrote each sample's \texttt{psmcfa}. For NA18507, NA19239 and NA12878, chromosome~\EsevenPilotChrom{} converted directly from the joint VCF gave byte-identical files. Every genome was fitted from its \texttt{psmcfa}; the default set of \EsevenDefault{} genomes, NA18507, NA19239 and NA12878 and others drawn by seed to make two per population, was also fitted by C psmc and from its VCFs with the masks and \opt{--bin-callable auto}; the first default genome of each population was also fitted with the first window split; and NA18507, NA19239 and NA12878 were bootstrapped (\EsevenBootReps{} replicates on \EsevenBootThreads{} threads). Population curves are the 10\%, 50\% and 90\% quantiles of $\log_{10}\Ne$ across individuals. For the comparison with Genome in a Bottle, NA12878's PASS records with a heterozygous genotype of single-base alleles were matched by position and alleles with the heterozygous single-nucleotide variants of HG001's GRCh38 v4.2.1 benchmark \citep{wagner2022} inside both the strict mask and the benchmark's regions (\EsevenGiabMb{}~Mb).

\paragraph{Software and computing.} The simulations and analyses used Python 3.13.13 with msprime 1.4.4, tskit 1.0.3, stdpopsim 0.3.0, NumPy 2.5.3, SciPy 1.18.1, pandas 3.0.6 and Matplotlib 3.11.2, and htslib and bcftools 1.24. \psmcrs{} 0.2.0 was built with rustc 1.99.0 and the release profile, without build flags; every \psmcrs{} fit used the AVX2--FMA kernels. C psmc was lh3/psmc 0.6.5-r74, from sources identical to its commit 82fa2ad, with \texttt{fq2psmcfa} from the same sources, built with gcc 11.4.1 and \texttt{-O3 -march=x86-64-v3 -ffp-contract=off}, whose output was byte-identical to that of the Makefile's \texttt{-O2} build (Supplementary Note~1, section~7); \texttt{generate\_\allowbreak multihetsep.py} came from msmc-tools \citep{msmctools}. The fits ran on the Ibex cluster of King Abdullah University of Science and Technology, on AMD EPYC 7702 nodes of 128 cores, and the figures were drawn from the tables on an Apple M1 Pro laptop. Every output has a provenance record of its command, settings, seeds, the checksums of its inputs and outputs, the identities of the tools and how the job ran.

\section*{Data availability}
The 1000 Genomes high-coverage VCFs are available from the International Genome Sample Resource (\url{https://www.internationalgenome.org}), the strict accessibility mask from the 1000 Genomes Project, and Genome in a Bottle's HG001 v4.2.1 benchmark from NIST. The \texttt{psmcfa} inputs of the \EsevenGenomes{} genomes are available at \placeholder{Zenodo DOI}; the manifest of their sources, commands and checksums, every fit, bootstrap and table, and the turtle and NA12878 \texttt{psmcfa} files of E2 are in the repository (\texttt{experiment/runs}, \texttt{experiment/real\_data}). \placeholder{Source of the turtle data.}
